rationale: A wins because it mostly keeps its hands on the facts while still finding distinct press lanes. Its “A 1,400-store Northeast coffee chain makes oat milk the default non-dairy pour” is careful; B’s “A 1,400-store coffee chain makes oat milk the default, not the upcharge” smuggles in a pricing claim the update never gave. That is not polish; that is how a decent foodservice angle gets killed in the first fact-check.
gaps_in_A: “Oatly launches its lowest-footprint product while closing a US plant” overclaims the update. The fact is 31% lower than the previous formula, not Oatly’s lowest-footprint product.
“which is rarer than a self-reported one” is unsupported color. Prove third-party LCA verification is rare in this category or cut it.

“What happens to the workers when Oatly shuts the plant” is useful defensive prep, but it is not pitchable until plant location, headcount, and timing exist. A should not count it casually as one of “Five viable shapes.”
gaps_in_B: “A 1,400-store coffee chain makes oat milk the default, not the upcharge” invents a no-upcharge claim. Default non-dairy does not mean surcharge-free.
“unprofitable plant-based companies retreat from sustainability spending” is a tidy narrative with no support in the update, and it assumes reformulation equals added spending.
“same quarter delivers a verified footprint reduction and a plant closure” compresses timing past the facts. The update says the operating loss was last quarter; the rollout and closure are current.

“If the LCA report and a named chain contact are not obtainable this week... pitch only the foodservice angle” contradicts its own proof standard. The foodservice angle collapses without the chain contact.
